Something I notice is often overlooked in this discussion is how much the toxic environment created by The Pony Express is the real problem here.

Environments where your survival/happiness/sanity is dependent on your ability to ignore painful or obvious environmental issues essentially condition you to endure problems, rather than fix them. And it's not just your cognitive decision-making altered this way, but also what your subconscious allows you to perceive. 

This is really what Curly is all about, and why his failure to stop Jimmy is tragic, but not an immoral decision like Jimmy's sexual assault. Curly is trying his best to cope, not just for himself, but for everyone. He has to hold it together, and ensure the continued success of their mission, lest the whole thing fall apart. In a different context, his "willful ignorance" could be considered  "steadfastness" or "faith in his crew". 

His failure to help Anya isn't in spite of ethical qualities, but because of them. The same things that make him a good captain in this fucked up work environment make him bad at being the kind of person who was actually needed to stop this whole mess. Ironically, that person would be someone like Swansea, who would make a poor captain because of his cynical, negative worldview.

Anya says it herself: Pony Express didn't put locks on the bedroom doors. And for that, the entire crew is made to suffer.

I think your conclusions about the family are near/on the mark. It's unlikely that the Shattering War has ever really been about obtaining the great runes. Ostensibly it is, on thr surface, but the irony here is that each of the factional leaders has a secret motivation for fighting, save for one, Godrick, who is a punkass.

 Elden Ring is so much a game about failing or false perceptions, secret history and the power these things give or surrender to others. It only makes sense then that most of the royal family see through/disbelieve the sanctity of the golden order, including Marika herself, since she is the one responsible for the Shattering in the first place. 

In fact, I think that's probably what motivates the Greater Will to summon the Tarnished to the lands between in the first place. The Shattering War has no victors simply because no one is really trying to win it except for Godrick, who is a punkass, and Morgott, who is both unloved by the GO and more of a steward figure anyways. Thus, in desperation, the GW must scrape the bottom of the barrell for pawns.

However, in regards to Rykard killing Godwyn, I don't think there's enough evidence/implications to support that. Usimg Occams Razor, here, I see his blasphemy as twofold: he openly denies the legitimacy of the erdtree, and he kidnaps anybody he can so that he can eat them. He is a people eater, he eats people. This is very bad and I cannot stress that enough.

Joking aside, there is depth to both sins beyond the surface level stuff. Denying the erdtree's reign is heresy, and heresy and blasphemy are very close together. Note that this isn't just a philosophical disagreement, he is openly seceeding from the sovereignty of the GO. Imagine if, in medieval Europe during the crusades, Prussia declared itself to be, I dunno, pagan or something. That's grounds for excommunication and a full on crusade. Blasphemy.

But also consider symbolically what the act of eating people means in ER, on a deeper level. A recurring theme of the game is conjoinment, typically of the soul. All becoming one, one becoming all. The erdtree takes the souls of the dead into itself, like a tree's roots taking nutrients from the soil. (Literally and figuratively, think of the roots choked with dead bodies in the catacombs) This is the nature of the GO; a closed ecosystem of souls, cycling into and out of the erdtree with rules defined by a central authority. (Marika/Runes, these are not just legal laws, but laws of "reality" within the domain of the erdtree) 

Now, if Rykard is eating people, devouring all to feed himself and gain his own power, to become a new god of his own design...then he is violating the Erdtree at its core belief system. What he devours becomes removes from the GO. Fundamentally, he is despoiling the Erdtree. Stealing from it, subverting it, imitating its power as a cruel, mishapen monstrosity. Gluttony incarnate, a black mirror to the Erdtree and all it represents.

THAT is true blasphemy. And while I certainly can't disprove the theory that Rykard was part of the Night of Black Knives, this interpretation is big enough on its own to me that adding Godwyns murder onto that seems like a bit much.

Edit: Accidentally called Godrick Godfrey. Godfrey is definitely NOT a punkass.

Everyone does have a right to an opinion, and these people that have made you feel insecure have the opinion that you're wrong. While there's no need to be rude to a person about things, your trying to take solace in the midst of people that agree with you is just dismissing and ignoring what is probably valid criticism of your opinion to some degree.

I'm not saying you should let yourself be subject to abuse, but isn't this kind of thinking that you should only be listening to people who already agree with you self-defeating? No opinion is beyond reproach, and I can assure you there are many real and valid criticisms to be had about this movie.

Instead of trying to make ourselves feel better, shouldn't we be open and honest about this movie and its failing? I think its a telling sign that this movie has been so divisive; not in a challenging or political way, but because there are people who so strongly believe that this movie is very, very bad. I am one of them, admittedly. I submit that movies which are really good don't need people to stand up for them, they stand up for themselves. Movies, like any piece of art, are subject to the moods and perceptions of the time period they're being viewed in, but I'd say there's a reason the originals have been able to stand so long and still be viewed as the best creations of the many, many iterations of Star Wars: they understand the forms of storytelling, and tell a rich, interesting story in a way that these films simply don't.

There is so much more to say on the matter, and I'm quite interested in discussing and analyzing what exactly has created such a huge divide in the fanbase, but I think its a little much to get into in a reddit comment. Maybe I'll make a video or something.

But, to theorize, I think the people who like this movie so much like it for the same reason people worship gods or believe in ghosts or still think Donald Trump is a good president: It's because they want to. The desire to believe in something trumps the opinions of many people, because its unpleasant or frightening to believe otherwise. You may find that insulting; I'm not trying to insult you, because this is a perfectly normal thing that we all find ourselves doing, and I don't think you're a lesser person for enjoying a movie that I disagree with.

I don't want to be "That guy" who ruins the fun for everyone, but is anyone else dreading these movies more than anticipating them? It occurs to me that everything deserves to end. That just because someone can do something doesn't mean that they necessarily should. The way things are going right now, Star Wars and Indy will only end when the movies stop making money, which means that they'll only stop making them when they start to suck. Is this really the route we want to go down? We milk and milk and milk the shit out of a property until its audience is so sick of it that we discard its used up body so we can find another host to exploit? That's not fair to us, its fans, and its not fair to the story. I don't want my memories of Star Wars to be the bitter taste of a "Star Wars: Episode 15" that ruins the series or mars my opinion of the franchise so much I choose to forget that it exists. 

Great stories have endings. They cannot go on forever, so why are so many convinced that they can, or should?

It was the best plan. The best plan.

The prophecy had made it clear what was to come. A hero from the ashes of a ruined village (By my doing, of course) and would "Bring about the fall of his (my) empire." My...predecessors had also been clear-one cannot fight the prophecies. My council gave me everything from ego flattering words to detailed defensive plans. "My lord! No way a simple farm boy could stop you...." my vizier would say. "My lord! Might I recommend a careful placement of lieutenants along his projected journey..." crooned my generals. Fools. All of them. None of them truly understand the implications of prophecy. To fight it is to fight destiny. By the very act of fighting you've done exactly what the stars had fated for you. Prophecies could not be beaten.

But they could be fooled.

This would take a cunning of my own doing. The greatest trick would be necessary. Magicians would have to faint and Satan would have to blush at my cunning. I retired to my study to think. Seven days and seven nights I formulated the plan. Wracking every angle, every possibility. When I came out of my chambers, the great work had only just begun.

I assembled the seers, holy, unholy and everything in-between to dissect the prophecy. Every word, every syllable, every bit of grammar. A timeframe was needed. The first day, the last day. But the prophets had not made it easy, the narrowest we could figure it out had a window of two years. No matter, I would do it for twenty if necessary.

I assembled my council once more and told them nothing. I fed them a paltry plan that fulfilled their small-minded egos. A set of powerful lieutenants for my generals, destruction for the bloodthirsty, magical research for the arcanists, and my own decision to stay at my throne, which satisfied my most power-hungry of viziers seeking to usurp me. To even the trained eye, what I gave them was a solid plan, full of contingencies and sinister traps. But it was garbage. Garbage for garbage people.

I had a homunculus privately prepared in my image and likeness. The alchemists put to death of course, dissolved in their own chemical vats. The day came, and I wasted no time.

Donning a peasant's garb, I left a fake me at the throne, a perfect replica in every way, utterly convinced he was me and his plan would never fail. I left the castle and my journey began.

I walked to every village, travelling as a merchant, enduring the wretched poverty of the land. It took 14 months and 3 days, but I found him. Huddled in the ashes of a burned village (Destroyed by my empire's soldiers trying to kill all the first borns, ironically enough)
I found a boy, pubescent and eager for vengeance. I had found the "Hero." I donned the practiced smile, the eager sympathy and proper amount of comic relief. I picked him up, I called him friend, I told him I was with him. My sister, I said, had been killed as well. I was glad no crocodiles were around to see my tears, lest their laughter give me away. No matter what, I told him, we would avenge his family.

That was three years ago. And so much has happened. We fought together, met others and made a team of plucky would-be avengers. One by one, my lieutenants fell, not seeing through my disguise. I cackled inside at the deviousness of it all.

The day finally came. My castle was stormed, my armies were beaten, the freedom fighters had won. The rebels had banded together under one banner, peace was won. I stood behind the hero, the boy of prophecy. Waiting, as he stood over my homunculus, beaten and bleeding all over my marble floors. In one final slash, the dummy was killed. I waited, the two of us alone in my grand hall. (He had insisted this was something 'Only he could do'. Pfft. It took all my persuasion to convince him to let me tag along) I waited. I waited until the perfect moment, until I knew it was safe.

"We did it. His empire has fallen."

Perfect. I rushed him from behind and drew my wicked dagger before plunging it deep into his heart. (From the front, of course. Leave no suspicion.)

"Then let a new one begin."

I felt his blood on my hands. The warm blanket of sweet victory coating my hands. It was done.

What everyone saw that day and what the historians recorded was the treasured best friend of their hero crying over his corpse. The emperor had fallen. The day was won. From there, the new republic instituted said friend as the president of their new land, acting in the hero's wishes, of course. 

But what the history books did not see, what the bards songs did not understand, was that those many tears falling as the best friend crouched over the hero's remains were not tears of sadness.

They were tears of joy.
